name: Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7

lead: Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 (sold as Rigin) is a lab-made peptide with a fatty acid tail, used in anti-aging and sensitive-skin products. People use it for smoother, calmer-looking skin. It is paired with palmitoyl tripeptide-1 in Matrixyl 3000.

It is described as an anti-inflammatory signal peptide: in lab models it is reported to reduce IL-6 release, which would mean less inflammation-driven collagen breakdown. Its effects in people have mostly been studied inside multi-ingredient products rather than on its own. Peptides in general are widely used in sensitive-skin products, per an analysis of 88 facial cosmetics.

paras: It is used in daily serums and creams, typically in blends with other peptides, and applied to the face and neck. Results from such products are usually judged over weeks to months.
Sold as a cosmetic ingredient; labels advise external use only and avoiding the eyes. No ingredient-specific safety data were found.

angle.text: Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 (Rigin) is an anti-inflammatory signal peptide in anti-aging and sensitive-skin products, aimed at smoother, calmer skin. It is reported in lab models to dampen IL-6, limiting inflammation-driven collagen breakdown. Little isolated human data exist.

lead: Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 (Pal-GQPR, also sold as Rigin) is a synthetic peptide of glycine, glutamine, proline and arginine attached to palmitic acid, used in anti-aging and sensitive-skin cosmetics. It is applied as a serum or cream ingredient with the aim of calming skin inflammation and supporting the collagen and basement-membrane structure so skin looks smoother and firmer.[1] It is described as an anti-inflammatory signal peptide and is the second peptide in Sederma's Matrixyl 3000 complex, alongside palmitoyl tripeptide-1.[1][2]

Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, reports that it decreases IL-6 secretion in laboratory models and promotes laminin and collagen VII production.[1] Peptides in general are widely used in sensitive-skin products: an analysis of 88 facial cosmetics found peptides in 17 percent, palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 among them, while noting that much of the supporting data sits in patents and supplier brochures rather than randomized placebo-controlled studies.[3]

Published human efficacy data specific to this peptide alone are limited. Studies of eye creams and serums have tested it in combination with other actives, and a 2026 study imaged how the Matrixyl 3000 peptides move into the outer skin layer.[2][4]

paras: The palmitoyl group, a 16-carbon fatty acid chain on the glycine end, raises lipophilicity to aid passage through the stratum corneum.[1] The same strategy is used for related cosmetic peptides: Wikipedia describes palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 (Matrixyl), launched by Sederma in 2000, as a five-amino-acid peptide attached to a 16-carbon fatty chain meant to help it cross the skin's lipid layers.[5] Grokipedia says palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 was introduced in the early 2000s as part of Matrixyl 3000 and appears in products from brands such as The Ordinary and Paula's Choice.[1]

It appears in multi-peptide formulations; a US drug-label listing for a stretch-mark cream names it alongside tripeptide-1, hexapeptide-9, acetyl tetrapeptide-9, palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 and acetyl hexapeptide-8.[6]

Sederma, the French cosmetic ingredient company, launched Matrixyl (palmitoyl pentapeptide-4) in 2000, and Grokipedia reports that palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 came in the early 2000s as part of the Matrixyl 3000 complex, paired with palmitoyl tripeptide-1.[5][1] Palmitoylated peptides became a common design for cosmetic peptides because the fatty-acid chain is intended to carry the peptide into the outer skin.[5][1] It is often sold under the name Rigin and appears on ingredient lists of anti-ageing and sensitive-skin serums.[1]

Reported laboratory effects include lowering IL-6 secretion after stressors such as UVB, and promoting basement membrane proteins such as laminin IV and V and collagen VII.[1] A 2015 study of dermal extracellular matrix and the epidermal-dermal junction used mass-spectrometric imaging, in vivo reflectance confocal microscopy, echography and histology to examine age-related changes and then tested a blend of palmitoyl oligopeptide and palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7; it found that selected matrix proteins were less abundant in aged skin explants than in young ones.[7]
A 2026 knowledge-graph and docking study screened peptide ingredients for type III collagen mechanisms in cosmetics.[8]

A 2026 study used time-of-flight and orbital-trapping secondary ion mass spectrometry to track cosmetic actives into the stratum corneum in three healthy female volunteers. Serums containing Matrixyl 3000 were applied for 0.5, 2 and 5 hours, and both peptides, palmitoyl tripeptide-1 and palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7, were detected in stratum corneum layers with signal decreasing with depth.[2]

Wikipedia and ingredient references describe peptides as signal molecules in anti-wrinkle products, and a review of sensitive-skin cosmetics found three of seven peptides in the products analysed worked by a neurotransmitter-inhibiting mechanism and three were signal peptides; only five had evidence supporting use in sensitive skin and only one clinical study included volunteers with sensitive skin.[3][5]

A 12-week clinical trial of a multi-component anti-aging eye cream containing yeast/rice fermentation filtrate, N-acetylneuraminic acid, palmitoyl tripeptide-1 and palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 assessed hydration (Corneometer), elasticity (Cutometer), photographs (VISIA) and collagen density (ultrasound), with dermatologists and participants rating efficacy at baseline and weeks 4, 8 and 12. The authors reported improvements in skin hydration (28.12 percent), elasticity (18.81 percent) and collagen production (54.99 percent), and fibroblast experiments showed increased collagen and elastin synthesis; because the cream contained several actives, effects cannot be assigned to one ingredient.[4] No trial of this peptide alone was found.

Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 is named on labels alongside palmitoyl tripeptide-1.[1][3] An analysis of 88 facial cosmetics found peptides in 17 percent of them, palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 among them, and also noted that much of the supporting evidence for peptides in sensitive-skin products rests on in vitro or manufacturer studies.[3] As a cosmetic ingredient it is sold over the counter in serums, creams and eye products, and some products list it in combination with several other peptides rather than on its own.[6][4]
